literature.ref: Boyd, Lankford, Loeb and Wyckoff (2005), 'The Draw of Home: How Teachers' Preferences for Proximity Disadvantage Urban Schools', Journal of Policy Analysis and Management 24(1): 113-132 (NBER WP 9953, Sept. 2003)
literature.read: NBER working paper PDF, text and Tables 2-5
facts: New York State, teachers entering public school teaching 1999-2002: 61% (60.8%) took their first job within 15 miles of their hometown and 85% within 40 miles (Table 2; 90% within 40 miles in New York City)

urban districts import teachers from the suburbs: 36% of urban teachers have a suburban hometown, 6% of suburban teachers an urban hometown; the ratio of suburban-hometown teachers taking a city job to city-hometown teachers taking a suburban job runs from 2.6 (Buffalo) to 7.5 (New York City) (p. 7)

literature.ref: Reininger (2012), 'Hometown Disadvantage? It Depends on Where You're From', Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis 34(2): 127-145
literature.read: not read directly: the figure is as summarised at https://www.deansforimpact.org/about/news-and-blog/2017/03/06/13-miles-the-inherent-localism-of-teaching
facts: NELS:88: the median distance between the high school a teacher attended in 10th grade and her residence eight years later is 13 miles, about a quarter of the distance moved by other professionals; 4 miles for teachers who grew up in dense cities

literature.ref: New York City Independent Budget Office, 'Where Do NYC's Teachers and Principals Live Compared With Where They Work?'
literature.read: the PDF could not be opened from this environment (the old IBO address now redirects to the IBO home page, ibo.nyc.gov); figures and the date (Aug. 15, 2013) as given in the search summary of the report
facts: school year 2011-12: 67% of 70,328 New York City teachers live within the five boroughs; 81% of Staten Island teachers live in the borough where they work, 57% of Brooklyn teachers; teachers in Queens and the Bronx are the most likely to live outside the five boroughs

literature.ref: Santelli and Grissom (2024), 'A Bad Commute: Travel Time to Work Predicts Teacher Turnover and Other Workplace Outcomes', AERA Open 10; working paper: EdWorkingPaper No. 22-691 (Dec. 2022), 'A Bad Commute: Does Travel Time to Work Predict Teacher and Leader Turnover and Other Workplace Outcomes?'
literature.read: EdWorkingPaper No. 22-691 (Dec. 2022), PDF text, pp. 10, 15, 16, 17, 22 (printed page numbers); the 0.8-1.0 percentage points per 5 minutes is as stated in the published AERA Open abstract (via search; the published article was not opened)
facts: Metropolitan Nashville Public Schools (countywide), 2008-09 to 2019-20, home and school addresses with HERE travel times: mean one-way commute 21.8 minutes for teachers (p. 10); 19% of teachers travel 30 minutes or more (p. 15; compare the PUMS share of 30 minutes or more, section 4, not the share above 30); teachers who live out of the county commute 13.8 minutes longer than those who live in it (p. 15)

working paper: teachers who commute 45 minutes or more each way are 10 percentage points more likely to transfer schools (overall rate 12%) and 3 percentage points more likely to exit the district (overall rate 7%) than teachers in the same school who commute 0-5 minutes (pp. 16-17); predicted transfer probability 8% against 18%, exit 8% against 11% (p. 22). Published version: each 5 minutes of one-way commute raises the transfer probability by 0.8-1.0 percentage points over most of the distribution

literature.ref: U.S. Department of Transportation (2016), 'The Value of Travel Time Savings: Departmental Guidance for Conducting Economic Evaluations, Revision 2 (2016 Update)', memorandum of Sept. 27, 2016
literature.read: read from a web.archive.org copy (transportation.gov refuses scripted requests)
facts: local personal travel (commuting included) is valued at 50% of hourly median household income ($56,516 / 2,080 = $27.20 in 2015), $13.60 an hour (Tables 1, 3, 4; text p. 11); plausible range 35%-60%, $9.50-$16.30 (Tables 2 and 5, pp. 14 and 19); business travel 100% of gross compensation, $25.40

literature.ref: NCES, Digest of Education Statistics 2017, Table 203.90, 'Average daily attendance (ADA) as a percentage of total enrollment, school day length, and school year length in public schools, by school level and state: 2007-08 and 2011-12' (source: SASS Public School Data File, 2007-08 and 2011-12)
facts: United States average of 179 days in the school year (SE 0.1) and 1,203 hours, 2011-12 (the table reports school year length for 2011-12 only; 2007-08 has attendance and hours per day, 6.6, only)
